notes.front: What is encryption at rest?
notes.back: Encryption that protects data stored on a disk (including solid-state drives) or on backup media.
notes.explanation: Google applies it at the storage layer to all data it stores, using 256-bit Advanced Encryption Standard.
notes.example: Like a safe in a shared warehouse: someone who carries off the whole safe still cannot read the papers inside without the combination.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Default encryption at rest”, “Default encryption at rest”
notes.evidence: Encryption at rest is encryption that is used to help protect data that is stored on a disk (including solid-state drives) or backup media. All data that is stored by Google is encrypted at the storage layer using the Advanced Encryption Standard (AES) algorithm, AES-256.

notes.front: What is a data encryption key (DEK) in Google’s storage systems?
notes.back: The key that encrypts one logical chunk of stored data; each chunk has its own individual data encryption key.
notes.explanation: Two chunks never share a DEK, even when the same customer owns both or they sit on the same machine.
notes.example: Like a hotel where every room has its own lock, so one lost key opens one room and not the whole floor.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Default encryption at rest”, “Encryption at the infrastructure layer”
notes.evidence: Each chunk is encrypted at the storage level with an individual data encryption key (DEK): two chunks won't have the same DEK, even if they are owned by the same customer or stored on the same machine.

notes.front: What is Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS)?
notes.back: A service for creating and managing cryptographic keys, for use in compatible Google Cloud services and in your own applications.
notes.explanation: With it you can generate software or hardware keys, import existing keys, or link keys held in a compatible external key manager.
notes.example: An invoicing app calls Cloud KMS to sign each invoice with a key the finance team created and controls.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Key Management Service overview”, “Cloud Key Management Service overview”
notes.evidence: Cloud Key Management Service (Cloud KMS) lets you create and manage cryptographic keys for use in compatible Google Cloud services and in your own applications. Using Cloud KMS, you can do the following: Generate software or hardware keys, import existing keys into Cloud KMS, or link external keys in your compatible external key management (EKM) system.

notes.front: What is a customer-managed encryption key (CMEK)?
notes.back: An encryption key that you own, which supported Google Cloud services use to protect your data at rest.
notes.explanation: It gives you greater control over the keys that encrypt your data and places a cryptographic boundary around that data.
notes.example: Like fitting your own padlock to a rented storage unit: the landlord still opens it for you on request, but only while your padlock allows it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)”, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)”
notes.evidence: Customer-managed encryption keys are encryption keys that you own. This capability lets you have greater control over the keys used to encrypt data at rest within supported Google Cloud services, and provides a cryptographic boundary around your data.

notes.front: What does Cloud KMS Autokey do?
notes.back: It automates CMEK provisioning: key rings and keys are generated on demand as part of creating a resource.
notes.explanation: The service agents that use the keys to encrypt and decrypt are granted the Identity and Access Management roles they need automatically.
notes.example: Like a hotel that cuts a room key at the moment a guest checks in, instead of guests ordering keys weeks ahead.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)”, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) with Cloud KMS Autokey”
notes.evidence: With Autokey, key rings and keys are generated on demand as part of resource creation, and service agents that use the keys for encrypt and decrypt operations are automatically granted the necessary Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles.

notes.front: What are Cloud HSM keys?
notes.back: Hardware keys generated in a cluster of hardware security modules, with Google Cloud managing the clusters for you.
notes.explanation: You still control the rotation period, Identity and Access Management roles and permissions, and the organisation policies that govern the keys.
notes.example: Like renting a room in a bank vault instead of keeping a safe at home: the bank runs the vault, you decide who holds the keys.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Key Management Service overview”, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEKs)”
notes.evidence: You can generate hardware keys in a cluster of FIPS 140-2 Level 3 Hardware Security Modules (HSMs). You have control over the rotation period, IAM roles and permissions, and organization policies that govern your keys. When you create HSM keys using Cloud HSM, Google Cloud manages the HSM clusters so you don't have to.

notes.front: What is a customer-supplied encryption key (CSEK)?
notes.back: Key material you store yourself and provide to Cloud Storage or Compute Engine when needed.
notes.explanation: Google Cloud does not store CSEKs in any way, and CSEK support is not a feature of Cloud KMS. CSEKs for Compute Engine are deprecated.
notes.example: Like handing a locksmith your own key each time a door must be opened, then taking it home again.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Key Management Service overview”, “Customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEKs)”
notes.evidence: Caution: Customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEKs) for Compute Engine are deprecated. For more information about alternatives, see CSEK deprecation in Compute Engine. Cloud Storage and Compute Engine can use customer-supplied encryption keys (CSEKs). With customer-supplied encryption keys, you store the key material and provide it to Cloud Storage or Compute Engine when needed.

notes.front: What is Secret Manager?
notes.back: A secrets and credential management service for storing and managing sensitive data such as passwords, certificates and keys for other services.
notes.explanation: Each secret is a global resource holding metadata and a collection of secret versions.
notes.example: An app reads its database password from Secret Manager at start-up instead of from a settings file kept in the code repository.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Secret Manager overview”, “Secret Manager overview”
notes.evidence: Secret Manager is a secrets and credential management service that lets you store and manage sensitive data such as API keys, usernames, passwords, certificates, and more. A secret is a global resource that contains a collection of metadata and secret versions.

notes.front: What is VPC Service Controls?
notes.back: A control that creates perimeters protecting the resources and data of Google Cloud services you specify, to reduce data exfiltration risk.
notes.explanation: It guards against accidental or targeted action by outsiders or insiders, for services such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery.
notes.example: Like a museum that lets visitors wander freely between galleries but checks every bag at the exit.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of VPC Service Controls”, “How VPC Service Controls reduces data exfiltration risks”
notes.evidence: VPC Service Controls helps protect against accidental or targeted action by external entities or insider entities, which helps to minimize unwarranted data exfiltration risks from Google Cloud services such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery. You can use VPC Service Controls to create perimeters that protect the resources and data of services that you explicitly specify.

notes.front: What does a service perimeter do by default?
notes.back: It allows free communication within the perimeter but blocks communication to Google Cloud services across it.
notes.explanation: It is a security boundary around Google Cloud resources, and it works specifically with Google Cloud managed services.
notes.example: Like a ship’s watertight compartment: water moves freely inside it, but the bulkhead stops it crossing into the next one.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of VPC Service Controls”, “Isolate Google Cloud resources into service perimeters”
notes.evidence: A service perimeter creates a security boundary around Google Cloud resources. A service perimeter allows free communication within the perimeter but, by default, blocks communication to Google Cloud services across the perimeter. The perimeter works specifically with Google Cloud managed services.

notes.front: What is context-aware access?
notes.back: Access to resources decided by client attributes such as identity type, identity, device data and network origin.
notes.explanation: Identity type distinguishes a service account from a user.
notes.example: Like a club door policy that looks at who you are and what you carry, not only whether you are standing in the queue.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of VPC Service Controls”, “How VPC Service Controls reduces data exfiltration risks”
notes.evidence: Context-aware access to resources is based on client attributes, such as identity type (service account or user), identity, device data, and network origin (IP address or VPC network).

notes.front: In Access Context Manager, what is an access level?
notes.back: A description of the requirements a request must meet to be honoured, based on its context.
notes.explanation: Examples of those requirements include device type and operating system, the source network address and user identity.
notes.example: Like a rule that only company laptops on the office network may open the payroll system.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Access Context Manager Overview”, “Access Context Manager Overview”
notes.evidence: Access levels describe the requirements for requests to be honored. Examples include the following: Device type and operating system IP address User identity

notes.front: What is Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP)?
notes.back: A central authorisation layer for web applications, so you can use application-level access control instead of relying on network-level firewalls.
notes.explanation: Access is decided per application and per user rather than by which network a request comes from.
notes.example: Like a receptionist who checks each visitor’s badge at every office door, instead of one guard at the car-park gate.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Identity-Aware Proxy overview”, “Identity-Aware Proxy overview”
notes.evidence: IAP lets you establish a central authorization layer for applications accessed by HTTPS, so you can use an application-level access control model instead of relying on network-level firewalls.

notes.front: What is Chrome Enterprise Premium?
notes.back: An offering that adds enterprise security to Chrome: configurable data loss prevention, real-time threat protection and context-aware access controls.
notes.explanation: Its data loss prevention controls actions such as copying, pasting, downloading and printing.
notes.example: A salesperson opens the customer list in the browser; the browser lets them read it but blocks printing it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Chrome Enterprise Premium overview”, “Chrome Enterprise Premium overview”
notes.evidence: Chrome Enterprise Premium enhances Chrome's built-in security for enterprises by providing: Configurable Data Loss Prevention: Prevent data leaks by controlling actions such as copying, pasting, downloading, and printing. Real-time Phishing, Malware, and Sandboxing Protection: Automatically detect and block phishing sites, malware, and unsafe downloads. Context-Aware Access Controls:

notes.front: What is the Organization Policy Service?
notes.back: A service giving centralised, programmatic control over an organisation’s Google Cloud resources.
notes.explanation: An organisation policy administrator uses it to configure constraints across the entire resource hierarchy.
notes.example: Like a city building code that every architect must follow, whatever an individual client asks for.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Organization Policy overview”
notes.evidence: The Organization Policy Service gives you centralized and programmatic control over your organization's Google Cloud resources. As the organization policy administrator, you can configure constraints across your entire resource hierarchy.

notes.front: In Organization Policy, what is a constraint?
notes.back: A particular type of restriction against a Google Cloud service or list of services: a blueprint of which behaviours are controlled.
notes.explanation: One constraint can target a single service or a whole list of services.
notes.example: Like a road-sign design saying “no vehicles over 3 tonnes”, which only applies once it is posted at a particular bridge.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Constraints”
notes.evidence: A constraint is a particular type of restriction against a Google Cloud service or a list of Google Cloud services. Think of the constraint as a blueprint that defines what behaviors are controlled.

notes.front: What happens to an action that violates an organisation policy in dry-run mode?
notes.back: The violation is audit-logged, but the action is not denied.
notes.explanation: This lets you see how a policy change would affect your workflows before it is enforced.
notes.example: Like a new speed camera that records speeding drivers for a month before any fines are issued.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Organization policies in dry-run mode”
notes.evidence: An organization policy in dry-run mode is created and enforced similarly to other organization policies, and violations of the policy are audit-logged, but the violating actions aren't denied. You can use organization policies in dry-run mode to monitor how policy changes would impact your workflows before they're enforced.

notes.front: What question do Cloud Audit Logs help you answer?
notes.back: “Who did what, where, and when?” within your Google Cloud resources.
notes.explanation: Google Cloud services write these logs to record administrative activities and resource access.
notes.example: Like a building’s visitor book that every door signs automatically, recording who came in, which room and at what time.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud services write audit logs that record administrative activities and resource access. You can use Cloud Audit Logs to answer "who did what, where, and when?" within your Google Cloud resources with the same level of transparency as in on-premises environments.

notes.front: What do Data Access audit logs record?
notes.back: Calls that read resource configuration or metadata, and user-driven calls that create, modify or read user-provided resource data.
notes.explanation: They cover access to the data itself, not only changes to how resources are set up.
notes.example: Like a library ledger of who borrowed which book, as opposed to a record of who rearranged the shelves.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “Data Access audit logs”
notes.evidence: Data Access audit logs are log entries written by API calls that read the configuration or metadata of resources. They are also written by user-driven API calls that create, modify, or read user-provided resource data.

notes.front: What does a software supply chain consist of?
notes.back: All the code, people, systems and processes that contribute to developing and delivering your software, inside and outside your organisation.
notes.explanation: It reaches beyond your own organisation, so outside software and systems you rely on are part of it too.
notes.example: An open-source date library your app imports, and the build server that packages it, are both links in your chain.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Software supply chain security”, “Software supply chains”
notes.evidence: A software supply chain consists of all the code, people, systems, and processes that contribute to development and delivery of your software, both inside and outside of your organization.

notes.front: What is Binary Authorization?
notes.back: A Google Cloud product for implementing software supply-chain security measures when you develop and deploy container-based applications.
notes.explanation: It applies to container-based applications specifically, during both development and deployment.
notes.example: Like a theatre stage door that admits only performers whose names are on the approved list.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Binary Authorization overview”, “What is Binary Authorization?”
notes.evidence: Binary Authorization is a Google Cloud product that you can use to implement software supply-chain security measures when you develop and deploy container-based applications.

notes.front: In Binary Authorization, what is an attestation?
notes.back: A certification that a specific container image has completed a previous stage, such as a build or a manual check.
notes.explanation: You configure the Binary Authorization policy to verify the attestation before the image may be deployed.
notes.example: Like a “passed inspection” stamp on a parcel that the next depot looks for before loading it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Binary Authorization overview”, “Attestations”
notes.evidence: An attestation certifies that a specific image has completed a previous stage, as described previously. You configure the Binary Authorization policy to verify the attestation before allowing the image to be deployed.

notes.front: What does Binary Authorization’s continuous validation do?
notes.back: It periodically checks that container images associated with running Pods conform to your policy, and logs any that do not.
notes.explanation: It works with check-based platform policies, which are in Preview, and writes a log entry in Cloud Logging for each image that does not conform.
notes.example: Like a hygiene inspector who revisits a restaurant after it has opened, not just before.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Binary Authorization overview”, “What does Binary Authorization do?”
notes.evidence: Monitor: You can configure continuous validation (CV) with check-based platform policies (Preview) to periodically monitor that container images associated with running Pods conform to a policy that you define. If images don't conform with the policy, CV produces log entries in Cloud Logging.

notes.front: What is Sensitive Data Protection?
notes.back: A service that helps you discover, classify and de-identify sensitive data inside and outside Google Cloud.
notes.explanation: It works on data held outside Google Cloud as well as inside it.
notes.example: Like a sniffer dog that finds where card numbers are hidden in a warehouse of files, then helps you black them out.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”
notes.evidence: Sensitive Data Protection helps you discover, classify, and de-identify sensitive data inside and outside Google Cloud.

notes.front: What does de-identification do in Sensitive Data Protection?
notes.back: It obfuscates instances of sensitive data, with methods such as masking, redaction and tokenisation.
notes.explanation: Other available transformation methods include bucketing and date shifting.
notes.example: Like blacking out names in a report before it goes to outside researchers.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”, “Sensitive data de-identification”
notes.evidence: The de-identification service lets you obfuscate instances of sensitive data. Various transformation methods are available, including masking, redaction, bucketing, date shifting, and tokenization.

notes.front: What is Security Command Center?
notes.back: A cloud-based risk management solution that helps security professionals prevent, detect and respond to security issues.
notes.explanation: Prevention, detection and response all fall within its scope.
notes.example: Like a building’s security control room, with screens from every camera and alarm in one place.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Security Command Center overview”, “Security Command Center overview”
notes.evidence: Security Command Center is a cloud-based risk management solution that helps security professionals to prevent, detect, and respond to security issues.

notes.front: A start-up keeps customer files in Cloud Storage and has configured nothing about encryption. An auditor asks whether the files are encrypted at rest. What is accurate?
notes.back: D: Yes: Google encrypts all customer content at rest by default, with no action needed
notes.choices:
A) Only for files uploaded over an encrypted connection
B) No: encryption at rest must be switched on for each bucket
C) Only if the bucket uses a customer-managed encryption key
D) Yes: Google encrypts all customer content at rest by default, with no action needed
notes.choicesExplained: B is wrong because no switch is needed. C is wrong because a CMEK adds control, not the encryption itself. A confuses encryption in transit with encryption at rest.
notes.explanation: Google encrypts all customer content at rest without any action from you, using one or more mechanisms.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Default encryption at rest”, “Default encryption of data at rest”
notes.evidence: Google encrypts all customer content stored at rest, without any action from you, using one or more encryption mechanisms.

notes.front: With Google’s default encryption, who owns and controls the keys, and what can you see of them?
notes.back: Google Cloud owns and controls them; you cannot view or manage them or review key usage logs.
notes.explanation: Data from several customers might also share the same key encryption key.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)”, “Default encryption with Google-owned and Google-managed encryption keys”
notes.evidence: Google Cloud owns and controls the keys used to encrypt your data. You can't view or manage these keys or review key usage logs. Data from multiple customers might use the same key encryption key (KEK).

notes.front: What must you enable to achieve logical data separation through encryption?
notes.back: Cloud Key Management Service.
notes.explanation: With default encryption, a logical data chunk might contain the data of several customers.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Default encryption at rest”, “Encryption at the infrastructure layer”
notes.evidence: A logical data chunk might contain the data of multiple customers. If you want to achieve logical data separation through encryption, you must enable Cloud Key Management Service.

notes.front: Where does Google store DEKs, and what are they wrapped with?
notes.back: Near the data they encrypt, wrapped by a key encryption key: the technique called envelope encryption.
notes.explanation: Keeping them near the data suits Google’s high volume of keys and its need for low latency and high availability.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Default encryption at rest”, “Key management”
notes.evidence: Because of the high volume of keys at Google, and the need for low latency and high availability, DEKs are stored near the data that they encrypt. DEKs are encrypted with (wrapped by) a key encryption key (KEK), using a technique known as envelope encryption.

notes.front: A colleague claims: “With default encryption, every Google Cloud customer gets its own key encryption key.” What is the correction?
notes.back: D: Key encryption keys exist per service, not per customer, and are held centrally in Keystore
notes.choices:
A) None: each customer has a dedicated key encryption key
B) Key encryption keys are held by the customer on premises
C) There are no key encryption keys; DEKs are stored unwrapped
D) Key encryption keys exist per service, not per customer, and are held centrally in Keystore
notes.choicesExplained: A repeats the mistake. B describes nothing in default encryption: Google owns those keys. C is wrong because DEKs are wrapped before storage.
notes.explanation: One or more key encryption keys exist for each service, and they are stored centrally in Keystore.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Default encryption at rest”, “Key management”
notes.evidence: These KEKs are not specific to customers; instead, one or more KEKs exist for each service. These KEKs are stored centrally in Keystore, a repository built specifically for storing keys.

notes.front: What are two uses of Cloud KMS keys besides encrypting and decrypting data?
notes.back: Creating or verifying digital signatures or message authentication code signatures, and establishing shared secrets with key encapsulation mechanisms.
notes.explanation: Signing, verification and key encapsulation are listed beside encryption among the uses of Cloud KMS keys.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Key Management Service overview”, “Cloud Key Management Service overview”
notes.evidence: Use Cloud KMS keys to create or verify digital signatures or message authentication code (MAC) signatures. Use Cloud KMS keys to establish shared secrets using key encapsulation mechanisms.

notes.front: Which option keeps data encrypted even while it is being processed, and is it part of Cloud KMS?
notes.back: Confidential Computing; it is not a feature of Cloud KMS.
notes.explanation: It encrypts data in use, keeping it private during processing.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Key Management Service overview”, “Confidential Computing”
notes.evidence: You can use the Confidential Computing platform to encrypt your data-in-use. Confidential Computing ensures that your data stays private and encrypted even while it's being processed. Note: Confidential Computing is not a feature of Cloud KMS.

notes.front: A bank’s rules say key material for its most sensitive workload must never be held by the cloud provider; it runs its own supported key manager. Which option fits?
notes.back: B: Cloud External Key Manager keys
notes.choices:
A) Google default encryption
B) Cloud External Key Manager keys
C) Cloud HSM keys
D) Keys created by Autokey
notes.choicesExplained: A uses keys Google owns. C and D keep key material in Google-run hardware security modules, even though you control the keys.
notes.explanation: External keys reside in a supported key manager outside Google Cloud, yet still secure your Google Cloud resources.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Key Management Service overview”, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEKs)”
notes.evidence: External keys and Cloud EKM - You can use keys that reside in an external key manager (EKM). Cloud EKM lets you use keys held in a supported key manager to secure your Google Cloud resources.

notes.front: A payments firm wants hardware keys in dedicated partitions it controls, with instance operations approved by a quorum of its own administrators. Which option fits?
notes.back: D: Single-tenant Cloud HSM
notes.choices:
A) Multi-tenant Cloud HSM keys
B) Customer-supplied encryption keys
C) Cloud KMS software keys
D) Single-tenant Cloud HSM
notes.choicesExplained: A shares Google-managed hardware security module clusters. C is software, not hardware. B keeps key material with the customer and works only for Cloud Storage and Compute Engine.
notes.explanation: Google Cloud still hosts the clusters, but the customer controls access and maintains the instance with its administrators.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Key Management Service overview”, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEKs)”
notes.evidence: When you create a Single-tenant Cloud HSM instance, Google Cloud hosts the HSM clusters so you don't have to, but you control access to the instance and maintain it with a quorum of designated administrators.

notes.front: Which role must a service’s service agent hold on a CMEK, and do the people reading the data need access to the key?
notes.back: CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter; requesters need no direct access to the CMEK.
notes.explanation: As long as the service agent holds that role, the service can encrypt and decrypt its data.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)”, “Manually creating CMEKs”
notes.evidence: For a requester to gain access to the data, they don't need direct access to the CMEK. As long as the service agent has the CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter role, the service can encrypt and decrypt its data.

notes.front: What happens to CMEK-protected data if you revoke the service agent’s role, or disable or destroy the key?
notes.back: The data can’t be accessed; some services can suffer permanent data loss if the key stays unavailable too long.
notes.explanation: The service agent decrypts on your behalf only while it has the role and the key is usable.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)”, “Manually creating CMEKs”
notes.evidence: As long as the service agent has the CryptoKey Encrypter/Decrypter role, the service can encrypt and decrypt its data. If you revoke this role, or if you disable or destroy the CMEK, that data can't be accessed. Caution: Some services can experience permanent data loss when the CMEK remains disabled or inaccessible for too long.

notes.front: A company wants its database administrators unable to manage the keys that protect their databases, while a security team manages keys. How should the CMEK key rings be placed?
notes.back: A: In a separate key project that only the security team administers
notes.choices:
A) In a separate key project that only the security team administers
B) Nowhere: use Google default encryption
C) In the same project, with a basic role for everyone
D) In each database project, with the administrators as key owners
notes.choicesExplained: D and C let the same people manage data and keys. B gives no customer control of keys at all.
notes.explanation: A separate project gives finer control of Identity and Access Management roles and supports separation of duties.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)”, “Manually creating CMEKs”
notes.evidence: Using different projects gives you greater control over IAM roles and helps support separation of duties.

notes.front: What are two limits CMEK organisation policy constraints can place on the keys used?
notes.back: Which Cloud KMS keys may be used, and where CMEKs may be located (among others).
notes.explanation: They give Organization Administrators controls to require CMEK usage as well as to limit the keys used.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)”, “CMEK organization policies”
notes.evidence: These constraints provide controls to Organization Administrators to require CMEK usage and to specify limitations and controls on the Cloud KMS keys used for CMEK protection, including the following: Limits on which Cloud KMS keys are used for CMEK protection Limits on the allowed protection levels of keys Limits on the location of CMEKs

notes.front: Is CMEK a different kind of encryption from Google’s default encryption?
notes.back: No: both are server-side, symmetric envelope encryption; CMEK differs in using a key the customer controls.
notes.explanation: The data path is the same; what changes is who controls the wrapping key.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)”, “What a CMEK-integrated service provides”
notes.evidence: Like Google Cloud's default encryption, CMEK is server-side, symmetric, envelope encryption of customer data. The difference from Google Cloud's default encryption is that CMEK protection uses a key that a customer controls.

notes.front: What is crypto-shredding, as a reason to use CMEK?
notes.back: Selectively deleting data protected by your keys, when off-boarding or to remediate security events.
notes.explanation: It is one of the goals Google lists for owning and controlling your own keys.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)”, “When to use customer-managed encryption keys”
notes.evidence: Selectively delete data protected by your keys in the case of off-boarding or to remediate security events (crypto-shredding).

notes.front: A regulator requires a fintech to log every administrative and data access to the keys protecting its customer records. It uses default encryption today. What should change?
notes.back: D: Protect the records with CMEKs in Cloud KMS
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: default encryption already gives customers key usage logs
B) Enable Data Access audit logs on the storage only
C) Move to customer-supplied encryption keys everywhere
D) Protect the records with CMEKs in Cloud KMS
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: you can’t review usage logs for Google’s default keys. C is wrong: CSEK support is not a Cloud KMS feature, Google Cloud does not store those keys, and only Cloud Storage and Compute Engine use them. B logs data access, not access to the keys.
notes.explanation: Logging administrative and data access to keys is one of the stated goals for CMEK.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)”, “When to use customer-managed encryption keys”
notes.evidence: Log administrative and data access to encryption keys. Meet current or future regulation that requires any of these goals.

notes.front: A platform team wants developers to get CMEKs when they create resources, without filing key requests in advance, while keeping separation of duties. What fits?
notes.back: D: Cloud KMS Autokey
notes.choices:
A) Customer-supplied encryption keys
B) Manually created keys in every developer project
C) Google default encryption
D) Cloud KMS Autokey
notes.choicesExplained: B needs key rings and keys planned and created before resources exist. C gives no customer-managed key. A is not a Cloud KMS feature and suits only two services.
notes.explanation: With Autokey the developer requests the key as part of resource creation.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)”, “Using Autokey for CMEK”
notes.evidence: Developers don't need to plan ahead to request keys prior to resource creation. They can request keys themselves from Autokey as needed, while still preserving separation of duties.

notes.front: Secret Manager versus Cloud KMS: in which can an authorised user view the stored value?
notes.back: Secret Manager: with permission you can view a secret’s contents. Cloud KMS: you can’t view, extract or export the key material.
notes.explanation: Secret Manager stores actual secret values; Cloud KMS stores keys and performs cryptographic operations with them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Secret Manager overview”, “Difference between secrets management and key management”
notes.evidence: Data stored Actual secret values. With the appropriate permissions, you can view the contents of the secret. Cryptographic keys. You can't view, extract, or export the actual cryptographic secrets (the bits and bytes) that are used for encryption and decryption operations.

notes.front: An app needs a database password and a partner’s access key at runtime. Developers currently paste them into a settings file. Where should they go?
notes.back: D: Secret Manager
notes.choices:
A) Cloud KMS, as encryption keys
B) Sensitive Data Protection
C) Instance labels on the servers
D) Secret Manager
notes.choicesExplained: A manages cryptographic keys you can’t read back, not stored credentials. B finds and masks sensitive data rather than serving it to apps. C is plain metadata, not a protected store.
notes.explanation: Storing configuration such as database passwords needed at runtime is Secret Manager’s typical use.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Secret Manager overview”, “Difference between secrets management and key management”
notes.evidence: Store configuration information such as database passwords, API keys, or TLS certificates needed by an application at runtime.

notes.front: A team must encrypt millions of rows in a database with keys whose raw material no one, including the team, can ever export. Which service fits?
notes.back: D: Cloud KMS
notes.choices:
A) Secret Manager
B) Binary Authorization
C) Security Command Center
D) Cloud KMS
notes.choicesExplained: A stores values that authorised users can read back. C manages risk findings, not keys. B controls which container images are deployed.
notes.explanation: Large encryption workloads, such as encrypting rows in a database, are a typical Cloud KMS use.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Secret Manager overview”, “Difference between secrets management and key management”
notes.evidence: Handle large encryption workloads, such as encrypting rows in a database or encrypting binary data such as images and files.

notes.front: An insider with valid credentials works in a project inside a perimeter that protects a sensitive BigQuery dataset. They try to copy a table to a dataset in a project outside the perimeter. Identity and Access Management would allow it. What happens?
notes.back: D: VPC Service Controls blocks the copy across the perimeter
notes.choices:
A) The copy succeeds because Identity and Access Management allows it
B) The copy succeeds but is flagged in Security Command Center
C) The copy is blocked only if an organisation policy forbids copying
D) VPC Service Controls blocks the copy across the perimeter
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores that the perimeter is independent of Identity and Access Management. B and C invent conditions: the perimeter blocks such service operations itself.
notes.explanation: The perimeter prevents copy operations to resources outside it, such as a public bucket or an external table.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of VPC Service Controls”, “Security benefits of VPC Service Controls”
notes.evidence: VPC Service Controls prevents service operations such as a gcloud storage cp command copying to a public Cloud Storage bucket or a bq mk command copying to a permanent external BigQuery table.

notes.front: Virtual machines in a VPC network outside a perimeter need to read a Cloud Storage bucket inside it. What must you configure?
notes.back: A: An ingress policy that allows those machines in
notes.choices:
A) An ingress policy that allows those machines in
B) An egress rule on the perimeter
C) Nothing: Identity and Access Management permissions are enough
D) A second perimeter around the machines
notes.choicesExplained: B covers clients inside reaching out, the opposite direction. C is wrong because the perimeter blocks the request whatever Identity and Access Management says. D adds a boundary rather than opening one.
notes.explanation: Without an ingress policy, machines outside the perimeter cannot reach buckets inside it.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of VPC Service Controls”, “Isolate Google Cloud resources into service perimeters”
notes.evidence: You must specify an ingress policy to allow VMs within VPC networks that are outside the perimeter to access Cloud Storage buckets that are inside the perimeter.

notes.front: Ingress rule versus egress rule in VPC Service Controls?
notes.back: Ingress: lets a client outside the perimeter reach resources inside. Egress: lets a client or resource inside reach Google Cloud resources outside.
notes.explanation: Direction is judged from the perimeter: ingress comes in from outside, egress goes out from inside.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of VPC Service Controls”, “Glossary”
notes.evidence: ingress rule A rule that allows an API client that is outside the perimeter to access resources within a perimeter. For more information, see Ingress and egress rules. egress rule A rule that allows an API client or resource that is inside the perimeter to access Google Cloud resources outside the perimeter.

notes.front: By default, can requests from the internet reach managed resources inside a service perimeter?
notes.back: No; they are denied unless ingress rules or access levels permit them based on the request’s context.
notes.explanation: Attributes such as source address, identity or source project can be used to allow them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of VPC Service Controls”, “Control access to Google Cloud resources from the internet”
notes.evidence: Access from the internet to managed resources within a service perimeter is denied by default. Optionally, you can enable access based on the context of the request. To do so, you can create ingress rules or access levels to permit access based on various attributes, such as the source IP address, identity, or source Google Cloud project.

notes.front: To reach resources in a perimeter privately from on-premises, which network must be part of the perimeter?
notes.back: The VPC network that contains the landing zone from on-premises.
notes.explanation: Only then can hosts in the on-premises network reach the perimeter’s resources privately.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of VPC Service Controls”, “Extend perimeters to an authorized VPN or Cloud Interconnect”
notes.evidence: To privately access Google Cloud resources within a perimeter, the VPC network that contains the landing zone from on-premises must be a part of the perimeter for resources in the on-premises network.

notes.front: Identity and Access Management versus VPC Service Controls: what kind of access control does each provide?
notes.back: Identity and Access Management: granular identity-based access control. VPC Service Controls: broader context-based perimeter security, including control of data egress.
notes.explanation: Google recommends using both together for defence in depth.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of VPC Service Controls”, “How VPC Service Controls reduces data exfiltration risks”
notes.evidence: While IAM enables granular identity-based access control, VPC Service Controls enables broader context-based perimeter security, including controlling data egress across the perimeter. We recommend using both VPC Service Controls and IAM for defense in depth.

notes.front: A bucket inside a perimeter has an allow policy that wrongly grants access to everyone. A request for it arrives from an unauthorised network on the internet. What does VPC Service Controls do?
notes.back: B: Denies it, because the network is not authorised
notes.choices:
A) Allows it, because Identity and Access Management is evaluated first and grants access
B) Denies it, because the network is not authorised
C) Allows it but writes a Data Access audit log
D) Deletes the faulty allow policy automatically
notes.choicesExplained: A and C assume Identity and Access Management alone decides. D describes something VPC Service Controls does not do.
notes.explanation: The perimeter is an extra layer that still denies unauthorised networks when Identity and Access Management is misconfigured.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of VPC Service Controls”, “Security benefits of VPC Service Controls”
notes.evidence: Public exposure of private data caused by misconfigured IAM policies: VPC Service Controls provides an extra layer of security by denying access from unauthorized networks, even if the data is exposed by misconfigured IAM policies.

notes.front: Identity and Access Management versus Organization Policy: which focuses on “who” and which on “what”?
notes.back: Identity and Access Management: who can take action on resources. Organization Policy: what restrictions apply to how resources can be configured.
notes.explanation: Identity and Access Management authorises actions based on permissions; Organization Policy restricts how specific resources can be set up.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Differences from Identity and Access Management”
notes.evidence: Identity and Access Management focuses on who, and lets the administrator authorize who can take action on specific resources based on permissions. Organization Policy focuses on what, and lets the administrator set restrictions on specific resources to determine how they can be configured.

notes.front: A company must stop anyone, including project owners, from creating resources outside approved regions. Which control fits?
notes.back: B: An organisation policy restricting resource locations
notes.choices:
A) A custom role without create permissions
B) An organisation policy restricting resource locations
C) A service perimeter around the approved regions
D) Data Access audit logs with alerts
notes.choicesExplained: A limits who, not where, and would block creation everywhere. C controls data movement between services, not where resources live. D only records what happened.
notes.explanation: Restricting the physical location of new resources is a listed use of organisation policies.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Common use cases”
notes.evidence: Organization policies allow you to do the following: Limit resource sharing based on domain. Limit the usage of Identity and Access Management (IAM) service accounts. Restrict the physical location of newly created resources.

notes.front: Which kind of organisation policy constraint is designed to replace legacy managed constraints?
notes.back: Managed constraints.
notes.explanation: They add flexibility and greater insight from Policy Intelligence tools, and Google manages them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Managed constraints”
notes.evidence: Managed constraints are designed to replace equivalent legacy managed constraints, but with additional flexibility and greater insight from Policy Intelligence tools. These constraints have similar structure to custom organization policy constraints, but are managed by Google.

notes.front: Which kind of organisation policy constraint is managed by your organisation rather than by Google?
notes.back: Custom constraints.
notes.explanation: Like managed constraints, they allow or restrict resource creation and updates.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Custom constraints”
notes.evidence: Like managed constraints, custom constraints allow or restrict resource creation and updates. However, custom constraints are managed by your organization instead of by Google.

notes.front: Which kind of organisation policy constraint uses list or boolean rules and was previously called “predefined”?
notes.back: Legacy managed constraints.
notes.explanation: The enforcing service evaluates the constraint type and value to decide what is restricted.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Managed constraints (legacy)”
notes.evidence: Legacy managed constraints have a constraint type of list or boolean, which determines the values that can be used for checking enforcement. The enforcing Google Cloud service will evaluate the constraint type and value to determine the restriction that is enforced. These legacy constraints were previously known as predefined constraints.

notes.front: Classify the constraint that disables serial port access on Compute Engine: list rule or boolean rule?
notes.back: Boolean rule: it is either enforced (serial port access not allowed) or not enforced.
notes.explanation: A list rule would instead hold allowed or denied values, such as project identifiers.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Boolean rules”
notes.evidence: A legacy managed constraint with a boolean rule is either enforced or not enforced. For example, constraints/compute.disableSerialPortAccess has two possible states: Enforced - the constraint is enforced, and serial port access is not allowed.

notes.front: By default, what do descendants of a resource with an organisation policy do?
notes.back: They inherit the organisation policy.
notes.explanation: Set on the organisation resource, a policy passes down through all descendant folders, projects and service resources.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Inheritance”
notes.evidence: When an organization policy is set on a resource, all descendants of that resource inherit the organization policy by default. If you set an organization policy on the organization resource, then the configuration of restrictions defined by that policy will be passed down through all descendant folders, projects, and service resources.

notes.front: An organisation-level policy blocks external addresses on virtual machines. One research folder has an approved need for them. What can be done?
notes.back: D: Set a policy on the folder that overrides the inherited one
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: organisation-level policies can never be changed lower down
B) Grant the researchers the Owner basic role
C) Move the folder outside the organisation
D) Set a policy on the folder that overrides the inherited one
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: descendants may overwrite inheritance. B is an Identity and Access Management change, and Identity and Access Management does not lift a constraint. C abandons central control instead of making a precise exception.
notes.explanation: Policies on descendants can overwrite or inherit the parent’s, which is how exceptions are made.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Inheritance”
notes.evidence: You can set an organization policy on a descendant resource that either overwrites the inheritance or inherits the organization policy of the parent resource.

notes.front: A new organisation policy restricts a state a resource is already in. What happens to that resource?
notes.back: It keeps its original behaviour; the policy is in violation and you must address it manually.
notes.explanation: This avoids a new policy completely shutting down business continuity.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Violations”
notes.evidence: If a new organization policy sets a restriction on an action or state that a service is already in, the policy is considered to be in violation, but the service won't stop its original behavior. You will need to address this violation manually. This prevents the risk of a new organization policy completely shutting down your business continuity.

notes.front: Security wants to restrict service account creation across the organisation but fears breaking delivery pipelines. What should it do first?
notes.back: B: Create the policy in dry-run mode and review the audit-logged violations
notes.choices:
A) Enforce it at once and fix pipelines as they fail
B) Create the policy in dry-run mode and review the audit-logged violations
C) Remove every service account role instead
D) Put all pipeline projects in a service perimeter
notes.choicesExplained: A risks the very outage they fear. C is an Identity and Access Management change with far wider effects. D controls data movement, not service account creation.
notes.explanation: Google recommends testing and dry-running every change to organisation policies.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Organization Policy overview”, “Policy Intelligence”
notes.evidence: We recommend that you test and dry-run all changes to your organization policies.

notes.front: Which role authorises a user to reach an IAP-secured web application?
notes.back: The IAP-secured Web App User role, on the project where the resource exists.
notes.explanation: After authentication, IAP applies the relevant Identity and Access Management policy to check that role.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Identity-Aware Proxy overview”, “Authorization”
notes.evidence: After authentication, IAP applies the relevant IAM policy to check if the user is authorized to access the requested resource. If the user has the IAP-secured Web App User role on the Google Cloud console project where the resource exists, they're authorized to access the application.

notes.front: IAP protects an app behind a load balancer with Compute Engine backends. A test shows another virtual machine in the project can reach the backends directly. What fixes this?
notes.back: A: Firewall rules that block backend traffic not coming through the load balancer
notes.choices:
A) Firewall rules that block backend traffic not coming through the load balancer
B) Grant the other machine’s service account the IAP-secured Web App User role
C) Turn IAP off and on again for the backend service
D) Enable Data Access audit logs on the project
notes.choicesExplained: C changes nothing about the direct path. B grants more access, not less. D records access but does not stop it.
notes.explanation: IAP does not protect against activity within a project; firewall rules are your responsibility.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Identity-Aware Proxy overview”, “Your responsibilities”
notes.evidence: If the backend resource is a VM, configure your firewall rules to protect against traffic that doesn't come through the load balancer. IAP doesn't protect against activity within a project, such as another VM inside the project.

notes.front: Several Cloud Run services in different regions sit behind one global load balancer, with IAP enabled on the load balancer. What gap remains?
notes.back: D: Each service’s automatically assigned address is not protected by IAP
notes.choices:
A) None: IAP now covers every path to the services
B) Users must now connect through a VPN
C) IAP cannot be used with Cloud Run at all
D) Each service’s automatically assigned address is not protected by IAP
notes.choicesExplained: A misses the direct address. C is wrong: IAP supports Cloud Run directly or behind a load balancer. B is wrong: IAP removes the need for a VPN.
notes.explanation: Only the load balancer path is protected in this set-up, so each service’s own address might be reached directly.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Identity-Aware Proxy overview”, “Authentication”
notes.evidence: Through a load balancer with a Cloud Run backend. This configuration is useful when you have multiple Cloud Run services in different regions behind a single global load balancer. In this configuration, the auto-assigned URL is unprotected by IAP and might be directly accessible.

notes.front: What does IAP’s context-aware access provide for virtual machines?
notes.back: Administrative remote access to machines in Google Cloud and other clouds, restricted to designated administrators by context.
notes.explanation: It covers machines in other clouds as well as in Google Cloud, with access limited by context.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Identity-Aware Proxy overview”, “Context-aware access”
notes.evidence: Virtual Machines (VMs) Enables administrative SSH/RDP access to VMs in Google Cloud and in other clouds. Lets you implement robust context-aware controls to restrict access to only designated administrators.

notes.front: Administrators need remote shell access to machines in Google Cloud and another cloud, limited to designated administrators on compliant devices, without a VPN. What fits?
notes.back: D: IAP with context-aware access for virtual machines
notes.choices:
A) Open the shell port to the internet with strong passwords
B) Cloud VPN from each administrator’s laptop
C) Secret Manager holding shared passwords
D) IAP with context-aware access for virtual machines
notes.choicesExplained: A exposes the machines to everyone. B is the VPN they want to avoid and does not check device context. C stores credentials but does not control access paths.
notes.explanation: IAP enforces access policies for applications and resources by identity and context.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Identity-Aware Proxy overview”, “When to use IAP”
notes.evidence: Use IAP when you want to enforce access control policies for applications and resources.

notes.front: Does Access Context Manager enforce access policy itself?
notes.back: No; it defines rules and context, and services such as VPC Service Controls enforce them.
notes.explanation: Enforcement happens at points such as VPC Service Controls, which apply the context it defines.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Access Context Manager Overview”, “Access Context Manager Overview”
notes.evidence: Access Context Manager isn't responsible for policy enforcement. Rather, Access Context Manager is designed to define specific rules or context. Policy is configured and enforced across various points, such as VPC Service Controls.

notes.front: After a new perimeter goes live, engineers can no longer use the Google Cloud console to view a bucket inside it. What is needed?
notes.back: B: An access level allowing their address ranges or user accounts
notes.choices:
A) The Owner basic role for each engineer
B) An access level allowing their address ranges or user accounts
C) An egress rule on the perimeter
D) Customer-managed encryption keys on the bucket
notes.choicesExplained: A is Identity and Access Management, which the perimeter checks independently. C lets clients inside reach out, not the engineers in. D changes key control, not network access.
notes.explanation: Console access to resources in a perimeter requires an access level for the engineers’ ranges or accounts.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Overview of VPC Service Controls”, “Control access to Google Cloud resources from the internet”
notes.evidence: To use the Google Cloud console to access resources within a perimeter, you must configure an access level that allows access from one or more IPv4 and IPv6 ranges, or to specific user accounts.

notes.front: Which two products does the Well-Architected Framework name as supporting its zero trust principle?
notes.back: Chrome Enterprise Premium and Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP).
notes.explanation: Zero trust means never trust, always verify: access depends on continuous verification of trust.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Well-Architected Framework: Security, privacy, and compliance pillar”, “Core principles”
notes.evidence: Implement zero trust: Use a never trust, always verify approach, where access to resources is granted based on continuous verification of trust. Google Cloud supports this principle through products like Chrome Enterprise Premium and Identity-Aware Proxy (IAP).

notes.front: Chrome Enterprise Core versus Chrome Enterprise Premium: which costs extra?
notes.back: Premium, which you upgrade to through sales. Core is included with Google Cloud at no additional cost.
notes.explanation: A 60-day trial of Premium is available before you commit.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Chrome Enterprise Premium overview”, “Upgrade to Chrome Enterprise Premium”
notes.evidence: Contact sales to upgrade to Chrome Enterprise Premium to get more information about upgrading from Chrome Enterprise Core to Chrome Enterprise Premium. A 60-day trial of Chrome Enterprise Premium is available. You can use Chrome Enterprise Core, which is included with Google Cloud at no additional cost.

notes.front: Contract staff must reach one internal web app hosted on Google Cloud from personal laptops, without a VPN, and only if the laptops meet a minimum security posture. What fits?
notes.back: C: Chrome Enterprise Premium
notes.choices:
A) Cloud VPN accounts for each contractor
B) A Shared VPC for the contractors’ laptops
C) Chrome Enterprise Premium
D) Cloud Audit Logs on the app’s project
notes.choicesExplained: A is the VPN they want to avoid and checks no device posture. B shares networks between projects, not with personal devices. D records access but does not gate it.
notes.explanation: Letting non-employees use personal devices that meet a minimum posture is a named Chrome Enterprise Premium use case.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Chrome Enterprise Premium overview”, “Common use cases”
notes.evidence: Allow non-employees to access data from their personal or mobile devices as long as they meet a minimum security posture.

notes.front: Which audit log type records user-driven calls that modify resource configuration or metadata, such as changing Identity and Access Management permissions?
notes.back: Admin Activity audit logs.
notes.explanation: They are always written: you can’t configure, exclude or disable them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “Admin Activity audit logs”
notes.evidence: Admin Activity audit logs are log entries written by user-driven API calls or other actions that modify the configuration or metadata of resources. For example, these logs record when users create VM instances or change Identity and Access Management permissions. Admin Activity audit logs are always written; you can't configure, exclude, or disable them.

notes.front: Which audit log type is written by Google Cloud systems rather than direct user action, for example when autoscaling adds machines to a MIG?
notes.back: System Event audit logs.
notes.explanation: They record configuration changes made by Google Cloud systems and managed service agents.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “System Event audit logs”
notes.evidence: System Event audit logs are log entries written by Google Cloud systems and managed service agents that modify the configuration of resources. System Event audit logs aren't driven by direct user action. For example, a System Event audit log is written when VMs are automatically added to or removed from managed instance groups (MIGs) due to autoscaling.

notes.front: Which audit log type is written when a service denies access because of a security policy violation?
notes.back: Policy Denied audit logs.
notes.explanation: They are generated by default, and your project is charged for storing them.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “Policy Denied audit logs”
notes.evidence: Policy Denied audit logs are log entries written when a Google Cloud service denies access to a user or service account because of a security policy violation. Policy Denied audit logs are generated by default and your Google Cloud project is charged for log storage.

notes.front: Are Data Access audit logs enabled by default?
notes.back: No, except for BigQuery; for other services you must enable them explicitly.
notes.explanation: They are off by default because they can generate large volumes of data.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “Data Access audit logs”
notes.evidence: Except for BigQuery, Data Access audit logs are disabled by default because they can generate large volumes of data. To record Data Access audit logs for Google Cloud services other than BigQuery, you must explicitly enable them.

notes.front: Logging is fully enabled. Which audit log would record that a user downloaded an object from a Cloud Storage bucket?
notes.back: B: Data Access audit logs
notes.choices:
A) Admin Activity audit logs
B) Data Access audit logs
C) System Event audit logs
D) Policy Denied audit logs
notes.choicesExplained: A covers changes to configuration or metadata. C covers changes made by Google systems. D covers access denied by a security policy.
notes.explanation: Reading user-provided resource data is recorded in Data Access audit logs, once enabled.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “Data Access audit logs”
notes.evidence: They are also written by user-driven API calls that create, modify, or read user-provided resource data.

notes.front: A developer changes an Identity and Access Management binding on a project. Which audit log records it, and can the log type be switched off?
notes.back: B: Admin Activity audit logs; cannot be disabled
notes.choices:
A) Data Access audit logs; off by default
B) Admin Activity audit logs; cannot be disabled
C) Policy Denied audit logs; can be disabled
D) System Event audit logs; always on
notes.choicesExplained: A covers reads and data access. D is for changes by Google systems, not users. C is for denied access, and it can’t be disabled either.
notes.explanation: Admin Activity logs are written even if the Cloud Logging interface is turned off.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Cloud Audit Logs overview”, “Admin Activity audit logs”
notes.evidence: Admin Activity audit logs are always written; you can't configure, exclude, or disable them. Even if you disable the Cloud Logging API, Admin Activity audit logs are still generated.

notes.front: How does Google’s payment-card compliance guide suggest keeping audit logs immutable for the long term?
notes.back: Store them in Cloud Storage with Bucket Lock, which can make objects immutable and undeletable for a set time.
notes.explanation: The retention time you set can range from seconds to years.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “PCI Data Security Standard compliance”, “Implementing immutable audit logging”
notes.evidence: Long-term, you can securely store immutable logs by using Cloud Storage bucket locks (section 10.3). Bucket locks let you set a policy to make all objects immutable and non-deletable for an amount of time that you specify, from seconds to years.

notes.front: Which framework does Google Cloud use to show the maturity level of your software supply chain security?
notes.back: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts.
notes.explanation: Google Cloud dashboards also show build provenance and vulnerabilities in build artefacts.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Software supply chain security”, “Safeguard software supply chains on Google Cloud”
notes.evidence: This information includes vulnerabilities in build artifacts, build provenance, and Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) dependency lists. Information identifying the maturity level of your software supply chain security using the Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts (SLSA) framework.

notes.front: A team relies heavily on open-source packages and wants ones Google has verified and tested, built in secure pipelines and regularly scanned. What fits?
notes.back: D: Assured Open Source Software
notes.choices:
A) Organization Policy Service
B) Binary Authorization
C) Sensitive Data Protection
D) Assured Open Source Software
notes.choicesExplained: B checks images at deployment but does not supply packages. C finds sensitive data, not vulnerable code. A restricts resource configuration.
notes.explanation: It secures the dependencies themselves, rather than checking images when they are deployed.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Software supply chain security”, “Protect the software supply”
notes.evidence: Assured Open Source Software provides open source packages that Google has verified and tested. These packages are built using Google's secure pipelines and are regularly scanned, analyzed, and tested for vulnerabilities.

notes.front: What does Binary Authorization do when an image fails its policy at deploy time?
notes.back: It blocks the deployment and writes a message to Cloud Audit Logs describing why.
notes.explanation: Images that pass the policy’s constraints are allowed to deploy.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Binary Authorization overview”, “Enforcement”
notes.evidence: If the image passes the constraints defined in the policy, Binary Authorization allows it to be deployed. If not, the service blocks deployment and writes a message to Cloud Audit Logs that describes why the image is out of compliance.

notes.front: What are the two attestation use cases Binary Authorization describes?
notes.back: Build verification, proving an image came from a specific build system or pipeline, and manual check, where a person creates the attestation.
notes.explanation: A build system can produce the attestation automatically, while a person such as a tester can create one by hand.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Binary Authorization overview”, “Attestations”
notes.evidence: in which Binary Authorization uses attestations to verify that an image was built by a specific build system or continuous integration (CI) pipeline. To learn how to set up a CI pipeline, based on Cloud Build, that can create an attestation, see Cloud Build integration. Manual check, where a person, for example, a QA representative, manually creates the attestation.

notes.front: A company must ensure that only images built by its approved pipeline and signed off by testers reach production GKE clusters. What fits?
notes.back: B: Binary Authorization requiring attestations
notes.choices:
A) A service perimeter around the clusters
B) Binary Authorization requiring attestations
C) An organisation policy on allowed regions
D) IAP in front of the clusters
notes.choicesExplained: A controls data movement between services. C limits where resources live, not what code runs. D controls who reaches applications, not which images deploy.
notes.explanation: Each attestation certifies a completed stage, and the policy verifies it before the image may deploy.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Binary Authorization overview”, “Attestations”
notes.evidence: An attestation certifies that a specific image has completed a previous stage, as described previously. You configure the Binary Authorization policy to verify the attestation before allowing the image to be deployed.

notes.front: Which Sensitive Data Protection service generates data profiles across an organisation, folder or project?
notes.back: The discovery service.
notes.explanation: Profiles hold metrics and metadata that show where sensitive and high-risk data reside.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”, “Sensitive data discovery”
notes.evidence: The discovery service lets you generate profiles for your data across an organization, folder, or project. Data profiles contain metrics and metadata about your data assets and help you determine where sensitive and high-risk data reside.

notes.front: Which Sensitive Data Protection service deep-scans one resource and reports every instance matching a chosen infoType?
notes.back: The inspection service.
notes.explanation: You choose which infoType it searches for, and the report covers each match.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”, “Sensitive data inspection”
notes.evidence: The inspection service lets you perform a deep scan of an individual resource to find instances of sensitive data. You specify the infoType that you want to search for, and the inspection service generates a report about every instance of data that matches that infoType.

notes.front: Which Sensitive Data Protection service analyses structured BigQuery data for the risk that information will be re-identified?
notes.back: The risk analysis service.
notes.explanation: It can be run before de-identification to plan the approach, or after it to watch for changes.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”, “Risk analysis”
notes.evidence: The risk analysis service lets you analyze structured BigQuery data to identify and visualize the risk that sensitive information will be revealed (re-identified). You can use risk analysis methods before de-identification to help determine an effective de-identification strategy, or after de-identification to monitor for any changes or outliers.

notes.front: What became of Cloud Data Loss Prevention?
notes.back: It is now part of Sensitive Data Protection; its programming interface kept the Cloud Data Loss Prevention name.
notes.explanation: Older material may still say Cloud Data Loss Prevention for the same capabilities.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”
notes.evidence: Cloud Data Loss Prevention (Cloud DLP) is now a part of Sensitive Data Protection. The API name remains the same: Cloud Data Loss Prevention API (DLP API).

notes.front: Researchers need a copy of clinic-visit records in which birth dates are shifted and ages grouped into bands, so no analyst sees exact values. Which capability fits?
notes.back: A: De-identification
notes.choices:
A) De-identification
B) Risk analysis
C) Discovery
D) Cloud KMS encryption
notes.choicesExplained: B measures re-identification risk but changes no data. C profiles where sensitive data sits. D hides everything from analysts rather than keeping the data usable.
notes.explanation: De-identification transforms identifiers, for example by date shifting or bucketing, so analysis can continue without plaintext personal data.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”, “When to use Sensitive Data Protection”
notes.evidence: De-identify analytical datasets while preserving utility: Transform direct and indirect identifiers using pseudonymization, date shifting, or bucketing so research and business intelligence teams can analyze data without exposing plaintext PII.

notes.front: Security must learn, at a high level and on a schedule, which BigQuery, Cloud SQL and Cloud Storage data across the whole organisation holds sensitive data. Which capability fits?
notes.back: D: Discovery (data profiling)
notes.choices:
A) An inspection job on one table
B) De-identification
C) Risk analysis
D) Discovery (data profiling)
notes.choicesExplained: A deep-scans a single resource. B changes data rather than finding it. C assesses re-identification risk in BigQuery data already chosen.
notes.explanation: Profiling scans large amounts of data at a high level; inspection gives instance-level detail.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Sensitive Data Protection overview”, “When to use Sensitive Data Protection”
notes.evidence: Discover shadow data across enterprise cloud repositories: Continuously scan and profile data assets across BigQuery, Cloud SQL, and Cloud Storage to locate uncatalogued sensitive data and evaluate organizational security posture.

notes.front: In Security Command Center, what is a finding?
notes.back: A record of a threat or other issue that a service has found in your cloud environments.
notes.explanation: Findings come from built-in, integrated and third-party security services.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Security Command Center overview”, “Security Command Center overview”
notes.evidence: Findings are records of threats or other issues that a service has found in your cloud environments. Findings are generated by the following sources: Built-in: Security services that are part of Security Command Center. Integrated: Google Cloud security services that integrate with organization-level activations of Security Command Center

notes.front: What is happening to Security Command Center’s Enterprise tier?
notes.back: It shuts down on 21 May 2027; organisations on it move automatically to the Premium tier on or after that date.
notes.explanation: The documentation already marks Enterprise as deprecated, beside the Standard-legacy, Standard and Premium tiers.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Security Command Center overview”, “Security Command Center overview”
notes.evidence: Standard-legacy, Standard, Premium, and Enterprise (Deprecated) service tiers The Security Command Center Enterprise service tier will shut down on May 21, 2027. If your organization uses the Enterprise service tier, then the organization will automatically move to the Premium service tier on or after May 21, 2027.

notes.front: A security lead wants one place to discover misconfigurations, publicly exposed resources and leaked credentials, and to detect active threats such as cryptocurrency miners. What fits?
notes.back: C: Security Command Center
notes.choices:
A) Organization Policy Service
B) Cloud Audit Logs
C) Security Command Center
D) Secret Manager
notes.choicesExplained: B records activity but does not detect problems for you. A prevents some configurations but does not discover threats. D stores credentials rather than finding leaked ones.
notes.explanation: Vulnerability detection and threat detection are both areas Security Command Center covers.
notes.source: Google Cloud documentation, “Security Command Center overview”, “Security Command Center overview”
notes.evidence: Vulnerability detection: Discover and remediate problems such as misconfigurations, publicly exposed resources, leaked credentials, and resources with known risks.
